stances.claim: Impeachment is a clear statutory exception to bank secrecy under RA 1405, making the Senate subpoenas legally proper; the defense fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree motion was correctly rejected because bank secrecy law does not bar admission of illegally obtained bank records and the signature card was not leaked by the government.
stances.rhetorical_move: two-ground rejection of the fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree motion

stances.claim: The Senate has a stronger argument for the dollar deposit disclosure than the single written-permission exception under RA 6426 suggests: the SC has already allowed such disclosure in Salvacion (1997) and China Banking (2006) to prevent perpetuation of injustice, and Corona constitutional obligation of public accountability overrides the absolute confidentiality rule.

Beyond the legal technicalities, Corona must demonstrate -- when he takes the stand -- the fitness, integrity, and moral ascendancy worthy of the highest judicial office, because he will be judged not merely on legal hermeneutics but on the much larger perspective of what is best for the country.

notable_anecdotes: Corona puzzling statement that the leaked specimen signature card could have come only from the PSBank -- which explains why he closed three PSBank peso accounts on the day of his impeachment -- making CJ wonder why his lawyers still filed the fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree motion if the leak was from the bank (not the government).
Corona national TV promise to bare his dollar accounts whether or not there will be a TRO -- CJ accepts at face value and says he should be given every opportunity to do so.

The Senate argument that the statutory rule on absolute confidentiality must yield to CJ Corona clear constitutional obligation -- framing RA 6426 confidentiality as a lesser statutory protection unable to override the constitutionally mandated SALN requirement.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains the legal framework for using bank deposits as evidence in the Corona impeachment trial. Under RA 1405 (Bank Secrecy Law), deposits are absolutely confidential with six exceptions -- including impeachment cases, making the Senate's subpoenas of PSBank and BPI for Corona's peso deposits legally proper. The defense filed a motion to suppress the peso deposits as the fruit of the poisonous tree (a rule coined by Justice Frankfurter and adopted by the Philippine SC in People v. Alicando, 1995) -- claiming the specimen signature card was illegally leaked to the prosecutors. The Senate rejected the motion on two grounds: bank secrecy laws do not bar admission of illegally obtained bank records, and there is no evidence the government leaked the card. CJ notes the puzzle: Corona himself said the source 'could have come only from the PSBank' -- explaining why he closed three PSBank peso accounts on the day of his impeachment, December 12, 2011 -- yet his lawyers still filed the motion. On the dollar deposits: RA 6426 (Foreign Currency Deposit Act) has only one exception (depositor's written permission); PSBank obtained a SC TRO barring disclosure. But the SC has previously allowed such examination in Salvacion v. Central Bank (1997) and China Banking v. Court of Appeals (2006) to 'prevent the perpetuation of an injustice'; and the Senate argues that 'the statutory rule on absolute confidentiality must yield to CJ Corona's clear constitutional obligation to fully declare and publicly disclose his assets.' PSBank president Pascual Garcia admitted the five dollar accounts belong to the CJ. CJ accepts at face value Corona's TV pledge to explain the accounts and calls on him to demonstrate -- before not just the impeachment court but the nation -- the fitness, integrity, and moral ascendancy worthy of the highest judicial office.
